references.text: Tax collectors came to John to be baptized, showing that they were open to his message—the same group that in Luke 7:29 justified God by being baptized.
Jesus says that tax collectors and prostitutes believed John, while the religious leaders did not repent—this aligns with the people and tax collectors justifying God through John's baptism.
The people from Jerusalem and all Judea went out to John and were baptized by him, which corresponds to the people's response described in Luke 7:29.
All the people were baptized, and Jesus himself was baptized—this confirms the broad response to John's baptism mentioned in Luke 7:29.
Direct contrast to verse 29: the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God's plan for them by refusing to be baptized by John.
David confesses that God is righteous in His judgment—to 'justify God' (dikaioo) as the people do in Luke 7:29 reflects this attitude of acknowledging God's righteousness.
Paul quotes Psalm 51:6 saying that God will be known as righteous—the same idea of justifying God found in Luke 7:29.
Tax collectors and sinners came to Jesus to hear him, showing the same openness among tax collectors described in Luke 7:29.
The tax collector who humbly asked for mercy was justified—this illustrates the same humble attitude that tax collectors showed when they justified God through John's baptism.
